title: Avoid eval on user-controlled input
corrected_pattern: Use ast.literal_eval only for simple trusted literal text, or parse expected values with explicit type checks.
explanation: Evaluating user-controlled text can execute arbitrary Python expressions in the current process context. This record treats eval on user input as a critical dynamic execution hazard.
safety_notes: Never use eval for user, file, network, or model-provided text. Prefer typed parsers, literal parsing for simple data, or explicit command maps.
verification_steps: Check official built-in function documentation for eval semantics before any status movement.

negative_tests: Reject any pattern where user input is passed directly or indirectly to eval.

title: Avoid exec on model-generated code
corrected_pattern: Map allowed operation names to reviewed functions and call only an explicitly selected function.
explanation: Executing model-generated code gives untrusted text process-level authority. Model output must remain data until reviewed and transformed through explicit, bounded operations.
safety_notes: Do not execute generated code from a model, prompt, file, network response, or user message. Use explicit dispatch tables and human review for any generated program text.

Confirm replacement logic uses explicit allowlisted operations.

title: Avoid compile with dynamic source text
corrected_pattern: Represent allowed behavior as structured data and interpret it with a small reviewed dispatcher.
explanation: Compiling dynamic source can prepare untrusted text for later execution. Even if compile does not execute immediately, it can become part of an unsafe eval or exec path.
safety_notes: Treat dynamic source as untrusted data. Avoid compile for user, model, file, or network input unless a separate sandbox and human review process exists.
verification_steps: Check official built-in function documentation for compile semantics before any status movement.
Confirm no later path feeds compiled objects to eval or exec.
Confirm structured data replaces source-code generation.

title: Avoid dynamic import from user-controlled module names
corrected_pattern: Resolve user choices through a whitelist such as {"json": "json", "csv": "csv"} before importing a known module.
explanation: A user-controlled module name can load unintended code or bypass an intended trust boundary. Dynamic import requires strict allowlisting and path hygiene.
safety_notes: Never import arbitrary user, file, network, or model-provided module names. Keep import targets explicit and review deployment search paths.

Confirm module names are selected from a fixed allowlist.
Confirm import path and package layout cannot be attacker-controlled.

title: Guard open with user-controlled write paths
corrected_pattern: Resolve the path under an approved base directory, reject traversal, validate the mode, and require explicit overwrite intent.
explanation: Opening a user-controlled path in a write mode can overwrite files, follow unsafe paths, or write outside the intended directory.
safety_notes: Use pathlib resolution, fixed base directories, explicit modes, encoding, and overwrite review. Treat write, append, and exclusive-create modes as separate risk cases.

Confirm path containment under an approved base directory.
Confirm write mode and overwrite intent are explicit.

title: Do not pass input into dynamic execution or shell commands
unsafe_or_wrong_pattern: value = input(); then pass value into dynamic execution or shell command construction
corrected_pattern: Parse input into a typed value or map it to a fixed allowlisted operation before any action is selected.
explanation: Raw input is untrusted. Passing it into dynamic execution, generated command strings, or shell-facing APIs creates injection risk.
safety_notes: Keep input as data. Validate type, range, and membership before use. Never treat a user-entered string as Python code or a shell command.

title: Avoid globals or locals for dynamic namespace mutation
corrected_pattern: Store dynamic values in an explicit dictionary owned by the application, such as state[allowed_name] = value after allowlist checks.
explanation: Mutating dynamic namespaces can obscure control flow, overwrite important bindings, and create injection paths when names are user-controlled.
safety_notes: Use explicit state dictionaries and allowlisted keys. Do not mutate interpreter namespaces from user, file, network, or model input.

title: Guard getattr, setattr, and delattr with user-controlled names
unsafe_or_wrong_pattern: getattr(obj, user_attr), setattr(obj, user_attr, value), or delattr(obj, user_attr)
corrected_pattern: Map user choices to a fixed set of allowed attribute names before reading or mutating an object.
explanation: User-controlled attribute names can expose internals, call unexpected descriptors, mutate security-sensitive state, or delete required object attributes.
safety_notes: Use explicit attribute allowlists. Treat mutation and deletion as higher risk than read access, and avoid dynamic access on privileged objects.

title: Never unpickle untrusted data
unsafe_or_wrong_pattern: pickle.load(file_obj) or pickle.loads(data) where the data is untrusted
corrected_pattern: Use json.loads with schema validation or another non-code-executing format for untrusted data.
explanation: Pickle is a Python object serialization format that can invoke code paths during loading. Untrusted pickle data is a critical deserialization hazard.
safety_notes: Do not accept pickle bytes or files from users, uploads, network peers, model output, or shared storage unless a separate trusted channel and review process exists.
verification_steps: Check official pickle documentation security warning before any status movement.

title: Avoid subprocess shell invocation with user or model input
unsafe_or_wrong_pattern: subprocess.run(command_text, shell=True) where command_text includes user or model input
corrected_pattern: Use subprocess.run([program, arg1, arg2], check=True, timeout=30) with validated arguments and no shell expansion.
explanation: Passing composed text to a shell can turn data into shell syntax. User or model-controlled fragments can alter the command that runs.
safety_notes: Prefer argument lists, fixed program names, explicit timeouts, and validated path or option values. Treat shell usage as exceptional and separately reviewed.
verification_steps: Check official subprocess documentation for shell behavior before any status movement.
Confirm command construction uses an argument list.
Confirm user or model input cannot alter the executable, options, redirection, or shell metacharacters.
negative_tests: Reject composed command strings containing untrusted input.
